suffer from a mathematical phenomenon known as "beta slippage" or volatility decay.1 
In volatile, oscillating markets, a leveraged ETF will inevitably lose value over time, even if the 
underlying reference index remains completely flat.1 For example, if an index drops 10%, a 3x 
leveraged bull ETF drops 30%. To recover to the original nominal value, the underlying index 
requires an 11.1% gain, but the leveraged ETF requires a 42.8% gain.1 This constant rebalancing 
drag guarantees structural decay.1 
Consequently, maintaining a long-term short position against a leveraged ETF is a 
mathematically advantageous strategy, almost guaranteeing a profit as the structural decay 
inherently benefits the short seller.1 However, achieving this in practice is immensely difficult.1 
Maintaining short positions requires locating and borrowing the underlying ETF shares from a 
prime broker.1 Because the institutional market widely understands the inevitable decay 
inherent in these funds, the borrow fees are universally exorbitant, sometimes exceeding 50% 
or even 100% annualized during peak volatility.1 These massive borrow costs effectively erase 
the mathematical profitability of the short trade.1 Bleich and Scout Trading devised an illicit 
mechanism to bypass these borrow costs entirely.1 
The Anatomy of the Naked Redemption Scheme 
Under the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation SHO, specifically Rule 204, 
broker-dealers are strictly prohibited from engaging in naked short selling.1 Before executing a 
short sale, a broker must have reasonable grounds to believe that the security can be 
borrowed and delivered on the settlement date—a fundamental market integrity mandate 
known as the "locate requirement".1 
Scout Trading deliberately, systematically, and repeatedly bypassed this requirement.1 The firm 
utilized Wedbush Securities Inc. (CRD No. 877) as its clearing firm, an entity that also served as 
an Authorized Participant (AP) for the targeted ETFs.1 An AP is a highly specialized financial 
institution permitted by the ETF issuer to create and redeem massive blocks of shares directly 
with the fund.1 
Scout Trading routinely submitted massive redemption orders to Wedbush Securities to 
redeem creation units of the leveraged ETFs.1 Crucially, the FINRA investigation proved that 
Scout Trading routinely submitted these redemption orders when the firm was insufficiently 
long the requisite number of ETF shares to actually satisfy the order.1 By simultaneously 
submitting these naked redemption orders to Wedbush and executing short sales of the ETF 
shares on the open secondary market, Bleich’s firm established massive short positions without 
actually locating, borrowing, or paying for the underlying securities.1 This generated significant 
proprietary profit for Scout Trading, driven by the economic decay of the ETFs, while 
completely shifting the systemic risk of the unsettled, phantom trades onto the clearing
